items.name: Language limits stated plainly
items.benefit: You know where checking is weaker outside English.
items.detail: Spoken-number reading and vocabulary hints work in English only. Numbers said in words in other languages may be flagged even when right.

categories.name: Models and hardware
categories.intro: Open models picked, pinned and tuned for the computer the clinic already owns, with optional graphics-card speed-ups.

items.name: First-run 'Download everything'
items.benefit: A new install gets to a working note with one button, and after that it works offline.
items.detail: About 6 GB (voice detection, Parakeet, the speaker models and Gemma 4 E4B) downloads smallest first, with one progress bar, the computer kept awake and a resumable Try again. The second recogniser for number checks is a separate download on the Models screen.
items.evidence: apps/desktop/src/components/SetupPanel.tsx; SetupPanel.test.tsx 'downloads every missing model, smallest first, then reports ready'; engine/os-engine/src/models.rs required_status; docs/plans/M1.md item 8

items.name: Model manager with a fit check
items.benefit: See which models suit this computer before downloading.
items.detail: Each model shows its use, size, licence and Fits, Tight or Won't fit, estimating its size plus about 25% against 90% of graphics memory, or against 70% of (RAM minus 4 GB) without a graphics card. Fits means at most 80% of that budget and Tight at most 105%, and models that won't fit can't be downloaded.

items.name: Model names explained in plain words
items.benefit: Vets who don't follow AI can understand names like 'gemma-4-12b-it-Q4_K_M'.
items.detail: Names become chips (12B, E4B, it, QAT, Q4_K_M, GGUF, MLX and others) with one-line meanings, a 9-term legend and a recommended size for this computer's memory. As a rule of thumb, E2B suits older laptops, E4B most computers and 12B cards with 10 GB or more, or Macs with 24 GB or more.

items.name: Browse Hugging Face from inside the app
items.benefit: Find and add other note-writing models, with licences checked before download.
items.detail: Search lists GGUF models, most downloaded first, pinned to their current version. Permissive licences such as Apache-2.0 or MIT download in one click, and restrictive or unstated ones must be accepted first.
items.evidence: engine/os-models/src/hub.rs (PERMISSIVE; tests restricted_licence_needs_acceptance, licences_are_classified); apps/desktop/src/screens/Models.tsx HubBrowser; docs/network.md R4

items.name: Restrictive licences only by choice
items.benefit: Restrictively licensed models are never slipped in; the clinic chooses them knowingly.
items.detail: A model with a restrictive or unstated licence found in the Hugging Face browser, such as one under Google's HAI-DEF terms, must be accepted before download and is kept out of the built-in list. A test checks the built-in list has only redistributable licences, with attribution in the licence notice file.
items.evidence: engine/os-models/src/hub.rs test licences_are_classified; engine/os-models/src/catalog.rs (line 160 and test only_redistributable_licenses_in_builtin_catalog); NOTICE

items.name: Pinned, verified, resumable model downloads
items.benefit: Every model is exactly the file that was tested, and multi-gigabyte downloads survive a dropped connection.
items.detail: 10 built-in models are each pinned to a Hugging Face revision with licence and attribution, and OpenBark's own downloader resumes and checks size, SHA-256 and free disk space. It was written because hf-hub 1.0 dropped resumable downloads.
items.evidence: engine/os-models/catalog.json (10 models); engine/os-models/src/download.rs; engine/os-models/src/store.rs test sha256_of_known_content; docs/plans/M0.md change 4

items.name: Choose the note model, or bring your own
items.benefit: Pick a faster or more careful model to suit the computer.
items.detail: An 'In use' panel picks the note model (Gemma 4 E4B by default) and shows the transcription and speaker models. Any .gguf model file can be used as well as the built-in ones.

items.name: 'MLX optimized' labels on the Mac
items.benefit: Mac users can see which models are MLX builds and aren't misled into downloading files the app can't run yet.
items.detail: On a Mac, the Hugging Face browser also lists MLX builds with a chip and a filter and points to the GGUF build that runs on the Mac's graphics chip today. Windows and Linux never list MLX builds.
items.evidence: docs/adr/0009-mlx-on-mac.md Decision 1; apps/desktop/src/screens/Models.tsx mlx-chip; docs/network.md R4

items.name: Graphics-chip drafting on every platform
items.benefit: The graphics chip is used for faster drafting wherever there is one.
items.detail: The installers draft with Metal on Apple silicon and Vulkan on Windows and Linux, including NVIDIA cards, and fall back to the processor. CUDA is used only when the browser version is built from source on a computer with NVIDIA's toolkit.
items.evidence: .github/workflows/release.yml (features: vulkan, metal); install/install.ps1 and install/install.sh (nvcc check); engine/os-llm/Cargo.toml

items.name: Optional speech pack for NVIDIA cards
items.benefit: On a Windows PC with an NVIDIA card, an 8.5-minute import is ready in about 43 s instead of about 150 s.
items.detail: Measured on an RTX 4080, the whole 8.5-minute import took 152 s on the processor and 43 s with the pack, and the number check kept pace. The pack downloads about 1.9 GB of runtime and 5.7 GB of full-precision models, resumably and checked, and Remove takes it away again.
items.evidence: docs/adr/0014-gpu-speech-recognition.md (table and Consequences); engine/os-models/src/gpu_pack.rs; apps/desktop/src/components/GpuCard.tsx; commit 3888f20

items.name: Graphics self-test in a separate process
items.benefit: A broken graphics driver can never crash the app; it stays on the processor and says why.
items.detail: After install and at each start, a separate process loads both models on the graphics card and transcribes a second of silence, and only a clean exit turns the card on. A failure shows Try again, and it was tested with every CUDA folder removed from the system path.

items.name: Speech pack state you can trust
items.benefit: The Models screen shows whether the graphics card is really in use, and Remove works in every state.
items.detail: Full precision is used only when CUDA really runs, an app update that changes the runtime is noticed, and download progress survives leaving the screen. A library of the same name that was there first is kept and put back.

items.name: Each recogniser on its fastest chip
items.benefit: Every speech model runs where it is quickest.
items.detail: The compact speech models stay on the processor (Parakeet took 43 s on the RTX 4080 against 28 s on 6 processor threads), and the full-precision builds use the graphics card. Whisper turbo at full precision took 166 s on the processor and 22 s on the card for 5.5 minutes of audio.

items.name: Choose where speech recognition runs
items.benefit: IT can force speech recognition onto the processor or the graphics card while troubleshooting.
items.detail: OPENBARK_ASR_PROVIDER (cpu, cuda or coreml) overrides the automatic choice. Core ML is accepted but hasn't been measured.

items.name: One inference engine of each kind
items.benefit: A stable app, free of crashes from clashing native libraries.
items.detail: Exactly one copy of llama.cpp's engine and at most one ONNX Runtime go into each program, checked in CI on Linux and macOS. whisper-rs was ruled out after it corrupted memory with a second copy.

items.name: Chat format read from each model
items.benefit: New model families work without code changes.
items.detail: Each model's own chat template, stored in its file, is used to talk to it. There are no hard-coded turn markers.

items.name: Hardware probe and benchmark
items.benefit: A clinic can see what its computer can run and measure speed on its own hardware.
items.detail: openbark probe reports memory, graphics card and processor features, and openbark bench measures time to first word, words per second and peak memory for each step. scripts/bench.sh runs a warm-up first and saves the results per computer and date.

items.name: Speech pack for Mac and Linux
items.benefit: Faster transcription could come to Macs and Linux PCs too.
items.detail: Core ML on the Mac hasn't been measured, and Linux CUDA needs its own pins and a test machine.

items.name: MLX engine on Apple silicon
items.benefit: Macs could run MLX models directly if they prove faster.
items.detail: This comes only after measuring llama.cpp on Metal against MLX for Gemma 4 E4B and 12B on the test consults. Until then the app says MLX models need this engine.

items.name: Model slots, profiles and your own model server
items.benefit: Clinics could swap each model separately or use a model server they already run.
items.detail: Planned: separate slots for transcription, notes, fast edits and speakers, profiles such as 'Laptop, balanced', and an optional OpenAI-compatible server. It would be off by default, clearly labelled and never a silent fallback.

categories.name: Speed and progress
categories.intro: Speed measured on one high-end Windows desktop so far, and named steps that tick off while you wait.

items.name: Note ready 13.1 s after stopping
items.benefit: The vet sees a draft within seconds of the consult ending.
items.detail: On a desktop with an RTX 4080 graphics card, a 9.6-minute test consult played in real time had its transcript complete 0.0 s after stop and its E4B note saved 13.1 s after stop, against a 30 s target. The same consult from a file took 76.8 s with E4B and 115.1 s with 12B on a shared graphics card.
items.evidence: docs/perf/M0.md 'Live recording' and stage tables; docs/perf/results/rtx4080-win11-20261017/

items.name: Import board with named steps
items.benefit: While a recording is imported or finished, you see each step tick off and how long is left.
items.detail: Reading the recording, Transcribing (minutes of audio done out of the total), Checking numbers with the second recogniser and Saving tick off under one bar that only moves forward, with an 'About n minutes left' estimate. The same board appears after you stop a live recording, and in the browser version uploading and in-browser conversion show as steps too.

items.name: Skipped steps explained
items.benefit: If a step doesn't apply, the board says why.
items.detail: When the second recogniser isn't installed, its step is marked skipped with 'Not installed: the Models screen can add it'. Skipped steps get their own icon, separate from finished ones.

items.name: Drafting board with each heading ticked
items.benefit: While a note drafts, you see which heading is being written and every step tick off.
items.detail: The board shows Loading the note model (only for the first draft after opening OpenBark), Reading the transcript with its line count, Writing the note with each heading ticked in turn, and Checking every number against the transcript. It shows the time so far and how long the last draft of this visit took.
items.evidence: apps/desktop/src/components/DraftProgress.tsx (DraftBoard); engine/os-engine/src/live.rs Stage (LoadModel, ReadTranscript, Write, Verify); engine/os-app/src/lib.rs load_llm_with_progress; apps/desktop/e2e/draft-board.mjs

items.name: Redrafts keep the current note visible
items.benefit: When you draft again, the current note stays on screen underneath until the new one is ready.
items.detail: The board names the template being used and says the current draft stays until the new one is ready, with earlier drafts kept. For a multi-pet visit it names the animal being drafted, such as Animal 1 of 2.

items.name: Progress for heading redrafts and client documents
items.benefit: Asking for a change to one heading, or drafting a client handout, shows its own progress board.
items.detail: A compact board sits inside the Ask panel while one heading is redrafted, and the client document panel shows a board with each heading of the handout. Step changes are announced to screen readers.

items.name: Faster structured drafting
items.benefit: The note structure is checked one word at a time, and fully only when a word breaks it. Checking every word in full was about 6 times slower with no gain in quality.
items.detail: The note structure is checked one word at a time and fully only when a word breaks it, which took E4B from 20.7 to between 45 and 58 tokens a second. Full checking was about 6 times slower with no gain in quality.
items.evidence: engine/os-llm/src/llama.rs; docs/perf/M0.md fixes table; docs/eval/M1.md finding 1

items.name: Processor threads tuned by measurement
items.benefit: Transcription on an ordinary processor runs at its fastest instead of slowing itself down.
items.detail: On 8.5 minutes of audio, 2 threads took 56 s, 4 took 34 s, 6 took 28 s, 8 took 39 s and 16 took 92 s. The main recogniser now uses a third of the processor (2 to 6 threads) and the second up to 8.
items.evidence: engine/os-asr/src/lib.rs (asr_threads, second_threads); docs/adr/0014-gpu-speech-recognition.md Context and Decision 1

items.name: Published speed measurements
items.benefit: Real timings from one high-end desktop with an RTX 4080, published with their caveats.
items.detail: On an RTX 4080, E4B read a 2,590-token prompt in 0.64 s and wrote 58 tokens a second with 3.4 GB peak memory, and 12B wrote 22 tokens a second with 7.2 GB. The graphics card was shared with a game, so these are treated as upper bounds.

items.name: 60-second drafting target on a Mac
items.benefit: A concrete speed target to confirm on Apple silicon.
items.detail: The target is a 10-minute consult drafted in 60 s or less, benchmarked on E4B and 12B. The Apple silicon run is still to do.

items.name: Clean benchmarks still to run
items.benefit: Remaining measurements are tracked in the open.
items.detail: A rerun on an idle graphics card, the Apple silicon benchmark, and the macOS disk image and uninstaller check are listed as pending.

categories.name: Installers and platforms
categories.intro: A desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux and a browser version for the same computer, installed with a double-click and removed without risk to the clinic's records.

items.name: Desktop app plus browser version
items.benefit: Use the installed app, or the same screens in a browser on the same computer.
items.detail: A desktop app built and tested on Windows, with macOS and Linux versions built but not yet tried on real machines. openbark serve runs the browser version locally with the same screens. After a folder change or speech pack install, the browser version offers Restart now and the desktop app restarts itself.
items.evidence: docs/adr/0004-monorepo-and-tooling.md; apps/desktop/src/engine.ts; docs/network.md R3; docs/adr/0013 Decision 7; docs/adr/0014 Decision 3

items.name: Windows setup wizard, no administrator needed
items.benefit: Installs like any Windows app, without IT rights.
items.detail: A per-user wizard in English, French, Spanish, German or Portuguese installs the program apart from the clinic's data. Uninstall is in the Start menu, and a newer setup updates in place.

items.name: Windows installer tested on a PC
items.benefit: Install, update and uninstall work cleanly, and uninstalling left 13.9 GB of data untouched.
items.detail: A silent install, an update in place and a silent uninstall were run, and the 13.9 GB data folder was byte-for-byte unchanged afterwards. The delete-data path waits for a separate test machine, since the development PC holds real data.

items.name: Uninstall keeps data unless you confirm twice
items.benefit: Uninstalling or updating can't wipe the clinic's visits by mistake.
items.detail: The 'Delete the application data' box is unticked by default and needs a second Yes or No that defaults to No. Silent and update uninstalls never delete data, and the script uninstaller asks you to type a confirmation word first.

items.name: Uninstall removes the speech pack; updates keep it
items.benefit: The large NVIDIA libraries don't linger after OpenBark is removed, and updating doesn't download them again.
items.detail: After the app has closed, the Windows uninstaller deletes exactly the files listed in the pack's manifest. An update leaves them in place.

items.name: Mac disk image with an uninstaller
items.benefit: Mac users get a drag-to-install image and a clear way to remove data if they choose.
items.detail: The image holds OpenBark, an Applications shortcut and an Uninstall OpenBark app that offers Keep my data (the default) or Delete my data with a second confirmation. The uninstaller's paths were tested with stand-in dialogs, and the real image is waiting for a test on a Mac.
items.evidence: scripts/macos-dmg.sh; install/macos/Uninstall OpenBark.app; docs/adr/0012 Decision 3; docs/runbooks/macos.md step 5

items.name: Linux .deb, .rpm and AppImage
items.benefit: Install from the Software app on Ubuntu, Debian, Mint, Fedora or openSUSE, or run the AppImage.
items.detail: Packages appear in the app menu, and removing them keeps data in ~/.local/share/OpenBark. They are built by the release workflow and are waiting for a hands-on test.

items.name: Release workflow builds every installer
items.benefit: All five installers (Windows setup, macOS disk image with its uninstaller, Linux .deb, .rpm and AppImage) come from one tagged build, and signing can be added once certificates exist.
items.detail: A version tag builds the Windows setup, the macOS disk image with its uninstaller, and the Linux .deb, .rpm and AppImage. The build fails if any installer is missing, and it can sign once certificates exist.

items.name: Install scripts for the browser version
items.benefit: Run OpenBark in a browser where the desktop app can't run.
items.detail: Double-click Install and Uninstall scripts build the browser version from source, choose the graphics option automatically and share the desktop app's data folder. CI checks that the .sh and .command scripts parse.
items.evidence: install/install.ps1; install/install.sh; install/README.md; .github/workflows/ci.yml 'Install scripts parse' (bash -n on install/*.sh and install/*.command)

items.name: WebView2 fetched only if missing
items.benefit: The Windows installer downloads nothing on a typical PC.
items.detail: Microsoft's WebView2 is downloaded only on a computer without it. The macOS image and Linux packages make no network calls.

items.name: Signed installers
items.benefit: Signing would remove the Windows and macOS security warnings on first open.
items.detail: Code signing and Apple notarisation wait on buying certificates. Until then the Mac app shows Open Anyway, and the release workflow can sign once certificates exist.

items.name: Phone apps
items.benefit: An iPhone app could record and transcribe the consult on the phone, with the note drafted on a computer. Android could follow.
items.detail: The iPhone app is designed: recording and transcription run on the phone, and drafting stays on computers. A test of background recording on the phone is designed with pass and fail criteria. No phone app has been built or tested yet.

items.name: Web app with models in the browser
items.benefit: A browser-only version could run Gemma 4 with WebGPU.
items.detail: A browser test and an installable web app are scheduled for a later milestone (M5).
items.evidence: docs/plans/M0.md item 6 (S3); the product brief section 6 (M5)

categories.name: Storage
categories.intro: The clinic decides where visits and models live, sees what will happen first, and moves data without risk.

items.name: Choose where models and visits are kept
items.benefit: Put models on a big drive and visits on a backed-up drive or clinic share.
items.detail: Settings shows each folder with its size and free space, and Change folder uses the system picker, or a small folder browser in the browser version. You can move what's there, use a folder as it is, or start empty.

items.name: Folder check before any change
items.benefit: The clinic sees exactly what will happen before data moves, and synced or removable drives are flagged.
items.detail: The check shows the exact folder and free space and warns about OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive or iCloud Drive folders and removable or network drives. It refuses the current folder, overlapping folders, folders inside the app's own data folder and folders OpenBark can't write to.
items.evidence: engine/os-models/src/locations.rs (synced_by); docs/adr/0013 Decision 3; commit 3888f20 ('Folders inside the app's data folder can't be chosen')

items.name: Cloud-synced folders stay private
items.benefit: A visits folder kept in OneDrive or Dropbox gives the sync service nothing it can read.
items.detail: Visits stay encrypted wherever they are kept, and the key stays on the computer. The sync service keeps copies it can't open.

items.name: Never mixed with other files
items.benefit: OpenBark's data is never spread among the clinic's other files.
items.detail: A chosen folder that already holds other things gets an 'OpenBark visits' or 'OpenBark models' folder inside it. A folder counts as OpenBark's only when everything in it is OpenBark's, so a move never sweeps up other files.
items.evidence: docs/adr/0013 Decision 4; commit 3888f20 ('A folder only counts as OpenBark's when everything in it is ours')

items.name: Safe move with rollback
items.benefit: Moving data can't lose or overwrite anything.
items.detail: On the same drive files are renamed instantly; across drives each is copied, checked and only then removed, with a progress bar, and a clash stops the move before anything changes. A failed copy is undone, and moves are refused while recording.
items.evidence: engine/os-models/src/locations.rs (move_tree and tests); apps/desktop/e2e/storage.mjs; docs/adr/0013 Decision 5

items.name: Folder changes wait for work to finish
items.benefit: Changing the data folder can't lose a draft, a signature or a patient being saved at the same moment.
items.detail: Imports, drafts, signing, edits, patient changes, downloads and recordings each hold a ticket, and a folder change is refused while any of them is writing. Late requests can't write to the old folder, and a move is put back if the new choice can't be saved.
items.evidence: commit 3888f20 ('Data safety: a work gate'); engine/os-app/src/lib.rs

items.name: Locations IT can fix
items.benefit: IT can set folder locations for managed installs.
items.detail: OPENBARK_MODELS_DIR, OPENBARK_SESSIONS_DIR and command-line options override the setting. Settings then shows 'Set by ...'.

items.name: Data kept apart from the program
items.benefit: Reinstalling or updating never touches the records.
items.detail: Data lives in the system's own app-data folder, apart from the program. Uninstallers never delete folders the clinic chose elsewhere.
items.evidence: install/README.md 'Your data, and the recovery key'; docs/adr/0013 Consequences

items.name: One folder per visit, re-runnable
items.benefit: Every recording, transcript and draft can be found again, replayed and redrafted, and nothing is overwritten.
items.detail: Each visit folder holds the visit's details, the audio, the transcript and numbered drafts, each with its note and template. The models and settings used are recorded too.

items.name: Imports kept as a playable recording
items.benefit: Any imported format can be replayed and redrafted later, even if the original file is gone.
items.detail: Every visit folder keeps the audio as an encrypted 16 kHz WAV, whatever format was imported.
items.evidence: commit 86d8e1b ('session folders always keep a 16 kHz WAV for playback'); engine/os-engine/src/vault.rs

items.name: Recordings are kept
items.benefit: Audio stays with the visit after signing, so a note can be checked or redrafted later.
items.detail: The brief's default of deleting audio at signing was changed so recordings are kept with their visit. They are removed only when their folder is deleted by hand or the app is uninstalled with its data.
items.evidence: docs/plans/M0.md decision 8 ('Retention changes from the master prompt'); engine/os-app/src/lib.rs (no delete-visit function)

items.name: Delete a visit, and a retention policy
items.benefit: Clinics will be able to delete a visit from the app and set how long recordings are kept.
items.detail: There is no delete button for a visit yet, in the app, the browser version or the command line. An optional auto-delete policy was planned in M0 and hasn't been built.

items.name: Show files
items.benefit: Open a visit's folder on disk straight from Review.
items.detail: Show files opens the visit folder in the system file manager. It is available in the desktop app.

categories.name: Design and accessibility
categories.intro: A calm, native-feeling interface that works by keyboard, screen reader and touch, in light or dark.

items.name: Apple-style design
items.benefit: The app feels native and calm on every platform.
items.detail: The system's own font, gentle spring motion, translucent materials for floating controls only, and grouped panels with rounded corners. Buttons give a small press response.

items.name: Follows reduced motion, transparency and contrast settings
items.benefit: The app respects the operating system's accessibility settings.
items.detail: Reduced motion swaps springs for short fades and stops the breathing ring, and reduced transparency makes frosted surfaces solid. Increased contrast strengthens borders and text.

items.name: Keyboard and screen reader support
items.benefit: Recording, drafting and signing can be done without a mouse and are announced to screen readers.
items.detail: WCAG 2.2 AA contrast, keyboard paths, visible focus rings, status shown as text as well as colour, and labelled icon buttons. Recording started, draft ready and note signed are announced aloud.
items.evidence: apps/desktop/src/App.tsx aria-live region; apps/desktop/src/components/NoteView.tsx; docs/design/STATUS.md 'Done' section 9

items.name: Progress announced to screen readers
items.benefit: Screen reader users hear what OpenBark is doing during long imports and drafts.
items.detail: Each progress board names its bar and reads out the current step and its detail. Step changes are announced as they happen.

items.name: Touch-friendly targets
items.benefit: Buttons are easy to hit on tablets and touch screens.
items.detail: Buttons, inputs and icon buttons are 44px on touch screens, and the Record button grows to 72px. Heading tools are always visible on touch.

items.name: Light, dark or system theme
items.benefit: Comfortable in a bright clinic or a dim imaging room.
items.detail: A System, Light or Dark switch in Settings follows the system by default. An explicit choice is remembered on the device.

items.name: Layouts for every window size
items.benefit: The layout fits a large monitor, a laptop or a narrow window.
items.detail: The sidebar becomes an icon rail below 1200px and a bottom tab bar below 640px, ready for the phone apps to come. The browser version runs on the same computer only, so phones can't open it today.
items.evidence: apps/desktop/src/app.css media queries; docs/network.md R3; docs/design/STATUS.md 'Done' section 4

items.name: Native-feeling sheets
items.benefit: Side panels behave like the sheets in native apps.
items.detail: On desktop, panels float inset; in narrow windows they become bottom sheets with a grabber that follows the finger and closes on a downward flick. Dialogs scale and fade.

items.name: Works offline: fonts and icons bundled
items.benefit: The interface looks right with no internet connection and calls no font servers.
items.detail: Geist fonts are bundled under OFL-1.1 as the fallback font, and Phosphor icons are bundled too. There is no emoji anywhere in the interface.

items.name: Plain clinical wording
items.benefit: Buttons and errors say what happens in plain veterinary English.
items.detail: Sentence case, buttons named for what they do, and specific error messages. 'Visit' replaced 'encounter' throughout the interface.

items.name: Tested interaction details
items.benefit: Buttons and panels behave predictably while work is running.
items.detail: Tests cover the record button being disabled while starting or stopping and sheets that ignore Escape while work runs. They also check that the theme follows the system and remembers an explicit choice.

items.name: Three-screen onboarding
items.benefit: New users could be guided through setup in three screens.
items.detail: Where to run, downloading models and recording consent. It is listed as not built yet.

categories.name: Developer and quality
categories.intro: Note quality is measured on realistic synthetic consults, every safeguard is pinned by tests on three platforms, and every decision is written down.

items.name: Note-quality evaluation
items.benefit: Every change to prompts or models is measured against consults with known facts before it ships.
items.detail: openbark eval drafts each synthetic consult and scores expected vitals, doses and phrases, invented numbers (a hard fail), citation errors and, in multi-pet visits, values in the wrong animal's note. Transcripts are cached, so a prompt change reruns only the note.

items.name: Synthetic consults with known answers
items.benefit: The scribe is tested on realistic consults without any real client's data.
items.detail: 14 recorded consults, 36 minutes in all, come from 13 scripts listing the expected facts, from canine wellness and feline vomiting to equine, exotics, oncology, production animal and surgery. Each has a reference file with speaker, text and timing.

items.name: Test voices made on the computer
items.benefit: New test consults can be voiced from a script, so coverage grows without recording real clients.
items.detail: A tool renders a script to audio plus its reference using Kokoro-82M (Apache-2.0), with a different voice for each speaker.

items.name: Example clinic notes for template tests
items.benefit: 'Template from an example note' is tested on notes written the way clinics chart.
items.detail: A SOAP note, feline dental charting by tooth and a cystotomy surgical report, each with its expected headings.

items.name: Speaker-label scoring
items.benefit: Speaker-label accuracy is measured against the truth.
items.detail: A script matches predicted segments to reference lines. It reports the speakers found and the share of speech given to the right speaker.

items.name: Whole-recording speaker separation for batch runs
items.benefit: Command-line batch runs split a finished recording by speaker, even with crosstalk and short interjections.
items.detail: The command-line transcribe, run, rerun, bench and eval paths use pyannote segmentation 3.0 with WeSpeaker fingerprints, numbering speakers in the order they first speak. The app's own imports use the live speaker tracker instead.
items.evidence: engine/os-cli/src/main.rs; engine/os-cli/src/sessions.rs; engine/os-diar/src/lib.rs (tests); engine/os-engine/src/transcribe.rs test speakers_renumbered_by_first_appearance

items.name: Batch speaker separation tuned by measurement
items.benefit: Two-person test consults are labelled as two people in batch runs, and labelling got faster.
items.detail: Raising the clustering threshold from 0.5 to 0.7 took the speakers found from 6 to the true 2, with 99.7% purity on the feline consult and 99.6% on the three-speaker multi-pet one. A window step of 0.25 instead of 0.1 cut labelling from 37.5 s to 14.9 s with identical purity.
items.evidence: docs/perf/M0.md 'Fixes made during the spike'; packages/eval/score_diarization.py

items.name: Recognition and speaker labelling side by side in batch runs
items.benefit: Command-line batch runs finish sooner because transcription and speaker labelling run at the same time.
items.detail: The wait is the longer of the two, not their sum: about 45 s together instead of about 84 s. The app's imports take the live path and don't use this.
items.evidence: docs/perf/M0.md stage and fixes tables; engine/os-engine/src/transcribe.rs (used by os-cli only)

items.name: Offline end-to-end test in CI
items.benefit: Every change proves the whole pipeline, from audio to a draft ready to sign, works with the network cut off.
items.detail: Linux CI runs transcription and drafting with networking disabled, first checking that huggingface.co can't be reached. It then requires a draft that passes the faithfulness check.

built_together.intro: OpenBark is built by the ANI.ML Health team, with veterinary input on every clinical decision. The aim is a scribe any clinic can trust: free, local and checkable.
practices: Every significant decision is written up as an architecture decision record, with the alternatives and their consequences.
Every network call the app can make is listed with what it sends and how to stop it.
Dependency and model versions are checked against their registries and pinned to exact versions.
Changes to speed or note quality are measured before and after, with zero invented numbers required every time.
Larger changes go through a multi-stage review, and every finding is checked before it is fixed.
Tests and help videos run on demo setups with their own made-up data, never real clinic data.
Known weaknesses and pending device tests are published alongside the results.
